title: Giant unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance enabled by hole-electron resonance in van der Waals heterostructures

paper_content.abstract: The hole-electron resonance in two-dimensional WTe2 dynamically screens the built-in electric field, disrupting the scattering equilibrium constraints of conventional electron transport. Here, we propose utilizing the hole-electron resonance to achieve Coulomb force-unconstrained spin angular momentum transfer across the WTe2/Fe3GaTe2 interface, offering a novel platform for exploring unconventional spin transport phenomena. A clear signature of this mechanism is the observation of an unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance of 289%, which far exceeds conventional spin Hall magnetoresistance and cannot be explained by standard spin absorption or scattering models. Its angular profile deviates from the simple cosine-squared form but realigns after accounting for magnetization and field orientation, reflecting the interplay between hole-electron resonance and magnetization dynamics. Furthermore, chiral transverse transport with distinct symmetry transitions emerges within the hole-active temperature regime, originating from interfacial symmetry breaking and the inhomogeneous spin-orbital coupling. These findings highlight the essential roles of both electrons and holes in spin transport.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors studied unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance (UAMR) of WTe2(9nm)/Fe3GaTe2(26 nm) heterostructure. The
main finding is the observation of an exceptionally huge UAMR of 289% at 5K when the magnetic field rotates in the yz-
plane (perpendicular to the current). Below 60K, more current (up to 90%) flows in Fe3GaTe2 layer. Significant UAMR was
observed below 100K. From the first-principles calculations, the authors showed a large spin-orbit coupling (SOC) exists in
WTe2 with the hybridization of W d-orbits and Te p-orbits. In addition, authors show the temperature-dependence of UAMR
follows a generalized logistic function. Large MR is a crucial quantity in spintronics that is important for magnetic sensing
and data storage. Thus, the topic is of great importance in the field of spintronics. I find the results also very interesting and
useful for the general readers of NC. However, I need to resolve some puzzles before making my formal assessment.
1) Large UAMR in WTe2 was already observed in Refs. 17-22. For example, even bigger UAMR was reported in Ref. 20. Is
not it nature to have large UAMR of WTe2(9 nm)/Fe3GaTe2(26 nm) heterostructure?
2) Huge MR in WTe2 was also attributed to the exact balance between electrons and holes in Ref. 17, the same as here in
addition to the SOC in WTe2. Other than SOC which I will also discuss below, I do not see the fundamental difference
between two mechanisms.
3) In terms of the role of SOC, I do not see how can it lead to large MR in general and UAMR in particular. Can authors
provide a convincing argument? I believe that it is important.
4) In Ref. 20, UAMR in WTe2 was claimed to be absolute cosine(\beta) not square of it although the data are similar. Authors
should compare their fitting and data against those in Ref. 20. It can help readers to have better understanding of the
systems.
5) It is also unclear to me how exact balance of electrons and holes and SOC leads to the specific expression of UAMR. A
quantitative sketch like what was done in Ref. 17 about large quadratic B dependence of MR from two carrier model.
Although two carrier model cannot really explain the linear MR reported in Ref. 20 and UAMR, it at least provides a possible
scenario for unsaturated quadratic B phenomenon. The manuscript will surely make a contribution to the field and the topic if
authors can do so.
6) It is not clear to me why Fig. 5d has the contribution from topological Hall effect (THE). THE is proportional to skyrmion
numbers. Can authors show the existence of skyrmions in their samples?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD), WTe2, has attracted a lot of attention as an ‘anomalous’ semimetal that exhibits
a striking linear magnetoresistance up to very high magnetic field. Various studies of the electronic states and electrical
transport in this material suggest that ‘electron-hole resonance’ (nearly balanced electron and hole populations) may be
responsible for the observed magnetotransport. The present manuscript aims to explore the effect of this
electron-hole resonance on spin transport. The motivation is not based on a rigorous theoretical prediction but rather relies on the intuitive
notion that spin transport under conditions of electron-hole resonance should yield interesting phenomena. There is a
reasonable rationale for this since all prior spintronics platforms have centered on materials wherein one carrier type
dominates. Thus, the theoretical analyses and fundamental understanding of spin scattering, spin
diffusion, spin accumulation etc. has generally been confined to the regime of single carrier types — or at best uncorrelated, single particle
physics of two carrier transport. Thus, the approach undertaken in this manuscript potentially offers an opportunity to open up a
new area for spintronics.
The key claim made here is the observation of a “giant” or “exceptionally large” and “unusual” anisotropic magneto-
resistance (AMR) in WTe2/Fe3GaTe2 hybrid heterostructures in the temperature window where electron-hole resonance
occurs. The authors draw this conclusion by measuring electrical transport as a function of magnetic field (orientation,
magnitude) and temperature. I would urge the authors to be cautious about the excessive use of such superlatives unless
the data clearly warrant it. For example, a reader of this manuscript will look at the data shown in Fig. 2 and wonder what (if
anything) is remarkable about the AMR of the hybrid WTe2/FGT devices when the control devices of purely WTe2 and FGT
show almost the same behavior. It is certainly true that there are qualitative differences in the dependence of the AMR on
magnetic field orientation (angle with current and sample plane), but the ‘large’ effect of “289%” is only revealed after
subtracting other contributions. The authors are to be commended for doing a careful job of analyzing the data and teasing
out the hidden physics. However, this does not warrant the use of hyperbole to describe the observations… If one aims to
exploit the claimed discovery of an “unusual” and “giant” AMR in this material system, the raw signal would need to have the
enhanced attributes. Even though there may be some very interesting physics lurking in the data shown here, the
observations do not show much chance of making any technological impact unless the phenomenon can stand on its own.
The authors also report the observation of chiral transverse transport in the hole-dominated regime. This is also (in principle)
quite interesting from a fundamental aspect and the authors accompany their observations with a DFT calculation that
potentially provides a foundation for understanding the phenomenon. The authors attribute ‘chirality’ to the interfacial
coupling between hole-electron resonance and magnetic moments or spin texture formation due to DMI. The authors also
mention that the chiral transport originates from the hybridization between the d-orbital of W and the p-orbital of Te, which
induces spatial symmetry breaking in the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) strength. However, this entire discussion is not very
clear or rigorous (e.g/ “This anisotropic SOC distribution could mediate anisotropic interactions ….” In the absence of a more
rigorous calculations, the use of illustrations or cartoons (in the supplementary) would be helpful.
Overall, the work presented here provides a first glimpse of spin transport and spin-charge interconversion in a previously
unexplored regime that combines several interesting factors arising from the presence of electron-hole resonance in a a
strongly spin-orbit coupled 2D material interfaced with a 2D ferromagnet. In principle, this could elicit broad interest because
of the potential implications for spintronics with 2D materials. The manuscript in its current form falls somewhat short of
achieving this goal. Drawing potentially impactful insights into spin transport in this interesting materials combination is
especially tricky since the claimed behavior does not really stand out in its own right but is rather subtly cloaked by other
transport contributions that are dominant even in the individual WTe2 and FGT. The authors would be well advised to stick
to clearly highlighting the novel aspects of the physics they are trying to reveal and avoid unnecessary hype with claims of
‘large’ effects without context. There should also be a high threshold to inventing new technical jargon such as “unusual
AMR” or UAMR. The term AMR is well understood by the spintronics community and the term “UAMR” as coined here is
imprecise and not particularly meaningful. There are also several detailed questions that need to be addressed before this
manuscript could be suitable for publication in Nature Communications. These are listed below. A major global concern is
that the conclusions drawn in this manuscript are based upon data on a single device (with measurements also shown on
two control devices). Were additional hybrid devices measured to make sure the observed unusual aspects of AMR are
reproducible? It is hard to imagine a paper such as this being published just based on results from a single device… Finally,
it would be helpful if the authors were to get the manuscript carefully proofed for typos, style, and language clarity. For
example, the grammatically incorrect use of the phrase “electron-dominate” in several figures (a better phrase “electron-
dominant” is used in the text in a couple of places; perhaps ‘electron-dominated” might be worth using instead). There are
other places where words are randomly capitalized. As it stands, the manuscript is very hard to read because of such
language issues and would not be suitable for Nature Communications without significant rewriting.
1. The specifications (dimensions) of the measured device are not explicitly provided. These should be mentioned
somewhere.
2. The measurement conditions mention a ‘small current’ of 10 microamps. Why is this current considered “small”? It would
be more meaningful to mention the current density and characterize its magnitude in the context of potential Joule heating.
Is there any Joule heating contribution to the observed AMR? (Nat. Commun. 9, 111 (2018))?3. As mentioned above, this work
explores a potentially new regime where spin-dependent transport is explored in the presence of electron-hole resonance.
However, it would be helpful if the authors could more precisely compare the quantitative and qualitative aspects of the AMR
found here compared to earlier work involving the same materials, specifically WTe2/CGT (Nature Materials 24, 1049–1057
(2025)) or other spin orbit coupled materials like topological insulators where an analogous effect, SMR, has also been
studied.
4. Both WTe2 and FGT are conducting, and most of the current flows through FGT presumably since this is about 3 times as
thick as the WTe2. (It would be helpful to have a comparison of the resistivity of the individual layers to estimate this current
distribution better.) How will the properties of the interface be decoupled from the bulk in the presence of these parallel
channels? The authors also conclude the AMR of the WTe2/FGT hybrid device contains features of both the individual
components. Since both components are conducting, shouldn’t this be expected? Similarly, if most of the current flows
through FGT, why would the observed AMR be absent in the hybrid device above 150K if it is present in the FGT?
5. What is the thickness of the control samples? Is it the same as that of the individual layers in the hybrid device? This does
not seem to be explicitly mentioned.
6. The temperature dependence of the AMR in the hybrid device resembles that of WTe2 even though most of the current
flows through FGT. This is perhaps worth dwelling on more deeply in the analysis and interpretation of the data. The abrupt
increase in the unusual component of AMR for WTe2/FGT below 150 K compared to only WTe2 below 80 K is striking. This
leads the authors to hypothesize that magnetic interactions have some influence on the charge carriers. This is a
reasonable conjecture but it would be useful to guide the reader toward ways in which this
hypothesis could be tested. Are magnetic interactions the only possible scenario? If so, what sets
the energy scale corresponding to 150 K where the effect turns on. It would also be useful to show
the T-dependent Rxx vs B data for the hybrid device.
7. Measurements of the Hall effect (Rxy) are always tricky because of unavoidable mixing of Rxx contributions into Rxy. The
usual approach is to antisymmetrize the data with respect to the magnetic field direction. The authors need to explain how
they accounted for any possible mixing of Rxx into Rxy. This could play an important role in interpreting signatures
associated with chirality.
8. It would be useful to extract the carrier type and density from the Hall data for some temperatures for the hybrid and control
samples.
9. The authors use Fig. 5 (c) to conclude that hole carriers predominantly contribute to the ordinary Hall effect. However, the
Rxy vs B is non-linear. Have the authors made a two carrier fit to extract information about multiple carrier contributions?
Could they provide estimates of the relevant characteristics (carrier density, mobility)? Given the parallel conduction
channels in this heterostructure, this is of course likely to be difficult to interpret but would be useful to know.
10. The authors refer to a ‘topological Hall effect’ with reference to Fig. 5 (d). However, this is far from clear: what aspects of
this data might lead the authors to claim the presence of a topological Hall effect? The most obvious signature of the
topological Hall effect is an excess Hall voltage above the anomalous and ordinary Hall effects. This has to be carefully
extracted and is not obviously present, even to an experienced eye. To make this attribution requires many more elaborate
tests.
11. The experimental section on the symmetry of Rxy needs to be more clearly written and needs more references. For
example, why are the experimental observations evidence of “chirality”? This is not at all clear. Also, what do the authors
mean by “higher order symmetry” in this context?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors have responded satisfactorily to the concerns that were raised in the first report by significantly revising relevant
parts of the manuscript and adding more data, particularly from additional samples/devices. In general, we believe that the
manuscript now conveys, with appropriate caveats, the introduction of a potentially interesting experimental platform for
studying spin transport effects in the presence of electron-hole resonance.
A primary concern raised in the first report still stands, namely, the continued emphasis on highlighting the large value of
UAMR at low temperature. Although this UAMR reaches 289%, this value is achieved only at 5 K, and it is not really
exceptional when placed in context of other MR effects in topological materials. For instance Cd₃As₂ exhibits spin Hall
magnetoresistance (SMR) of 68% at low temperatures (Phys. Rev. B 97, 201110(R), 2018), ZrTe₅ shows 43% (Phys. Rev. B
98, 121108(R), 2018), β-Ag₂Te shows 40% at room temperature (Nat. Commun. 15, 1259, 2024). These are smaller, no
doubt, than the UAMR observed here but still significant. In any case, the emphasis on large values in terms of percentage is
not particularly meaning full without some context... The primary advance that ought to be highlighted is suggested by the
sentences in the abstract: "Here, we propose utilizing the hole-electron resonance in WTe2 to achieve Coulomb force-
unconstrained spin angular momentum transfer across the magnetic heterojunction interface, offering a novel platform for
exploring unconventional spin transport phenomena. Within this framework, a large unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance
(UAMR) of 289% is observed in the plane perpendicular to 16 the charge current, far exceeding conventional spin Hall
magnetoresistance (SMR) and cannot be explained by standard spin absorption or scattering models." The authors would
be advised to revise this section in the abstract as follows: "Here, we propose utilizing the hole-electron resonance in WTe2
to achieve Coulomb force-unconstrained spin angular momentum transfer across the magnetic heterojunction interface,
offering a novel platform for exploring unconventional spin transport phenomena. A clear signature of this mechanism is the
observation of an unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance (UAMR) of 289% in the plane perpendicular to the charge current.
The value of this UAMR far exceeds conventional spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR) and cannot be explained by standard
spin absorption or scattering models." We believe this more precisely conveys the true scientific advance made in this
manuscript.
In addition, there are a couple of important issues that remain to be addressed.
1. The authors now show I–V characteristics in Fig. S3(a). This is useful but raises a new concern: the data is restricted to
the current range of 5 μA to 20 μA, and notably, does not intersect with the origin. This strongly suggests that the contacts
may be non-ohmic, which could significantly influence the interpretation of the transport measurements. It would be
important to clarify whether this behavior arises from contact resistance or some other mechanism.
2. The temperature dependence of UAMR has been fitted using a “generalized logistic function.” It would be helpful to
provide a physical justification for using this specific functional form. Is the choice of this model based on an underlying
theoretical framework, or is it purely empirical? Clarifying this point would strengthen the interpretation of the temperature-
dependent behavior.

### Reviewer 4

The transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD), WTe2, has attracted a lot of attention as an ‘anomalous’ semimetal that exhibits
a striking linear magnetoresistance up to very high magnetic field. Various studies of the electronic states and electrical
transport in this material suggest that ‘electron-hole resonance’ (nearly balanced electron and hole populations) may be
responsible for the observed magnetotransport. The present manuscript aims to explore the effect of this
electron-hole resonance on spin transport. The motivation is not based on a rigorous theoretical prediction but rather relies on the intuitive
notion that spin transport under conditions of electron-hole resonance should yield interesting phenomena. There is a
reasonable rationale for this since all prior spintronics platforms have centered on materials wherein one carrier type
dominates. Thus, the theoretical analyses and fundamental understanding of spin scattering, spin
diffusion, spin accumulation etc. has generally been confined to the regime of single carrier types — or at best uncorrelated, single particle
physics of two carrier transport. Thus, the approach undertaken in this manuscript potentially offers an opportunity to open up a
new area for spintronics.
The key claim made here is the observation of a “giant” or “exceptionally large” and “unusual” anisotropic magneto-
resistance (AMR) in WTe2/Fe3GaTe2 hybrid heterostructures in the temperature window where electron-hole resonance
occurs. The authors draw this conclusion by measuring electrical transport as a function of magnetic field (orientation,
magnitude) and temperature. I would urge the authors to be cautious about the excessive use of such superlatives unless
the data clearly warrant it. For example, a reader of this manuscript will look at the data shown in Fig. 2 and wonder what (if
anything) is remarkable about the AMR of the hybrid WTe2/FGT devices when the control devices of purely WTe2 and FGT
show almost the same behavior. It is certainly true that there are qualitative differences in the dependence of the AMR on
magnetic field orientation (angle with current and sample plane), but the ‘large’ effect of “289%” is only revealed after
subtracting other contributions. The authors are to be commended for doing a careful job of analyzing the data and teasing
out the hidden physics. However, this does not warrant the use of hyperbole to describe the observations… If one aims to
exploit the claimed discovery of an “unusual” and “giant” AMR in this material system, the raw signal would need to have the
enhanced attributes. Even though there may be some very interesting physics lurking in the data shown here, the
observations do not show much chance of making any technological impact unless the phenomenon can stand on its own.
The authors also report the observation of chiral transverse transport in the hole-dominated regime. This is also (in principle)
quite interesting from a fundamental aspect and the authors accompany their observations with a DFT calculation that
potentially provides a foundation for understanding the phenomenon. The authors attribute ‘chirality’ to the interfacial
coupling between hole-electron resonance and magnetic moments or spin texture formation due to DMI. The authors also
mention that the chiral transport originates from the hybridization between the d-orbital of W and the p-orbital of Te, which
induces spatial symmetry breaking in the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) strength. However, this entire discussion is not very
clear or rigorous (e.g/ “This anisotropic SOC distribution could mediate anisotropic interactions ….” In the absence of a more
rigorous calculations, the use of illustrations or cartoons (in the supplementary) would be helpful.

unexplored regime that combines several interesting factors arising from the presence of electron-hole resonance in a a
strongly spin-orbit coupled 2D material interfaced with a 2D ferromagnet. In principle, this could elicit broad interest because
of the potential implications for spintronics with 2D materials. The manuscript in its current form falls somewhat short of
achieving this goal. Drawing potentially impactful insights into spin transport in this interesting materials combination is
especially tricky since the claimed behavior does not really stand out in its own right but is rather subtly cloaked by other
transport contributions that are dominant even in the individual WTe2 and FGT. The authors would be well advised to stick

‘large’ effects without context. There should also be a high threshold to inventing new technical jargon such as “unusual
AMR” or UAMR. The term AMR is well understood by the spintronics community and the term “UAMR” as coined here is
imprecise and not particularly meaningful. There are also several detailed questions that need to be addressed before this
manuscript could be suitable for publication in Nature Communications. These are listed below. A major global concern is

reproducible? It is hard to imagine a paper such as this being published just based on results from a single device… Finally,

The authors studied unusual anisotropic magnetoresistance (UAMR) of WTe2(9nm)/Fe3GaTe2(26 nm) heterostructure. The

### Reviewer 4

The transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD), WTe2, has attracted a lot of attention as an ‘anomalous’ semimetal that exhibits
a striking linear magnetoresistance up to very high magnetic field. Various studies of the electronic states and electrical
transport in this material suggest that ‘electron-hole resonance’ (nearly balanced electron and hole populations) may be
responsible for the observed magnetotransport. The present manuscript aims to explore the effect of this
electron-hole resonance on spin transport. The motivation is not based on a rigorous theoretical prediction but rather relies on the intuitive
notion that spin transport under conditions of electron-hole resonance should yield interesting phenomena. There is a
reasonable rationale for this since all prior spintronics platforms have centered on materials wherein one carrier type
dominates. Thus, the theoretical analyses and fundamental understanding of spin scattering, spin
diffusion, spin accumulation etc. has generally been confined to the regime of single carrier types — or at best uncorrelated, single particle
physics of two carrier transport. Thus, the approach undertaken in this manuscript potentially offers an opportunity to open up a
new area for spintronics.
The key claim made here is the observation of a “giant” or “exceptionally large” and “unusual” anisotropic magneto-
resistance (AMR) in WTe2/Fe3GaTe2 hybrid heterostructures in the temperature window where electron-hole resonance
occurs. The authors draw this conclusion by measuring electrical transport as a function of magnetic field (orientation,
magnitude) and temperature. I would urge the authors to be cautious about the excessive use of such superlatives unless
the data clearly warrant it. For example, a reader of this manuscript will look at the data shown in Fig. 2 and wonder what (if
anything) is remarkable about the AMR of the hybrid WTe2/FGT devices when the control devices of purely WTe2 and FGT
show almost the same behavior. It is certainly true that there are qualitative differences in the dependence of the AMR on
magnetic field orientation (angle with current and sample plane), but the ‘large’ effect of “289%” is only revealed after
subtracting other contributions. The authors are to be commended for doing a careful job of analyzing the data and teasing
out the hidden physics. However, this does not warrant the use of hyperbole to describe the observations… If one aims to
exploit the claimed discovery of an “unusual” and “giant” AMR in this material system, the raw signal would need to have the
enhanced attributes. Even though there may be some very interesting physics lurking in the data shown here, the
observations do not show much chance of making any technological impact unless the phenomenon can stand on its own.
The authors also report the observation of chiral transverse transport in the hole-dominated regime. This is also (in principle)
quite interesting from a fundamental aspect and the authors accompany their observations with a DFT calculation that
potentially provides a foundation for understanding the phenomenon. The authors attribute ‘chirality’ to the interfacial
coupling between hole-electron resonance and magnetic moments or spin texture formation due to DMI. The authors also
mention that the chiral transport originates from the hybridization between the d-orbital of W and the p-orbital of Te, which
induces spatial symmetry breaking in the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) strength. However, this entire discussion is not very
clear or rigorous (e.g/ “This anisotropic SOC distribution could mediate anisotropic interactions ….” In the absence of a more
rigorous calculations, the use of illustrations or cartoons (in the supplementary) would be helpful.
Overall, the work presented here provides a first glimpse of spin transport and spin-charge interconversion in a previously
unexplored regime that combines several interesting factors arising from the presence of electron-hole resonance in a a
strongly spin-orbit coupled 2D material interfaced with a 2D ferromagnet. In principle, this could elicit broad interest because
of the potential implications for spintronics with 2D materials. The manuscript in its current form falls somewhat short of
achieving this goal. Drawing potentially impactful insights into spin transport in this interesting materials combination is
especially tricky since the claimed behavior does not really stand out in its own right but is rather subtly cloaked by other
transport contributions that are dominant even in the individual WTe2 and FGT. The authors would be well advised to stick
to clearly highlighting the novel aspects of the physics they are trying to reveal and avoid unnecessary hype with claims of
‘large’ effects without context. There should also be a high threshold to inventing new technical jargon such as “unusual
AMR” or UAMR. The term AMR is well understood by the spintronics community and the term “UAMR” as coined here is
imprecise and not particularly meaningful. There are also several detailed questions that need to be addressed before this
manuscript could be suitable for publication in Nature Communications. These are listed below. A major global concern is
that the conclusions drawn in this manuscript are based upon data on a single device (with measurements also shown on
two control devices). Were additional hybrid devices measured to make sure the observed unusual aspects of AMR are
reproducible? It is hard to imagine a paper such as this being published just based on results from a single device… Finally,
it would be helpful if the authors were to get the manuscript carefully proofed for typos, style, and language clarity. For
example, the grammatically incorrect use of the phrase “electron-dominate” in several figures (a better phrase “electron-
dominant” is used in the text in a couple of places; perhaps ‘electron-dominated” might be worth using instead). There are
other places where words are randomly capitalized. As it stands, the manuscript is very hard to read because of such
language issues and would not be suitable for Nature Communications without significant rewriting.
1. The specifications (dimensions) of the measured device are not explicitly provided. These should be mentioned
somewhere.
2. The measurement conditions mention a ‘small current’ of 10 microamps. Why is this current considered “small”? It would
be more meaningful to mention the current density and characterize its magnitude in the context of potential Joule heating.
Is there any Joule heating contribution to the observed AMR? (Nat. Commun. 9, 111 (2018))?3. As mentioned above, this work
explores a potentially new regime where spin-dependent transport is explored in the presence of electron-hole resonance.
However, it would be helpful if the authors could more precisely compare the quantitative and qualitative aspects of the AMR
found here compared to earlier work involving the same materials, specifically WTe2/CGT (Nature Materials 24, 1049–1057
(2025)) or other spin orbit coupled materials like topological insulators where an analogous effect, SMR, has also been
studied.
4. Both WTe2 and FGT are conducting, and most of the current flows through FGT presumably since this is about 3 times as
thick as the WTe2. (It would be helpful to have a comparison of the resistivity of the individual layers to estimate this current
distribution better.) How will the properties of the interface be decoupled from the bulk in the presence of these parallel
channels? The authors also conclude the AMR of the WTe2/FGT hybrid device contains features of both the individual
components. Since both components are conducting, shouldn’t this be expected? Similarly, if most of the current flows
through FGT, why would the observed AMR be absent in the hybrid device above 150K if it is present in the FGT?
5. What is the thickness of the control samples? Is it the same as that of the individual layers in the hybrid device? This does
not seem to be explicitly mentioned.
6. The temperature dependence of the AMR in the hybrid device resembles that of WTe2 even though most of the current
flows through FGT. This is perhaps worth dwelling on more deeply in the analysis and interpretation of the data. The abrupt
increase in the unusual component of AMR for WTe2/FGT below 150 K compared to only WTe2 below 80 K is striking. This
leads the authors to hypothesize that magnetic interactions have some influence on the charge carriers. This is a
reasonable conjecture but it would be useful to guide the reader toward ways in which this
hypothesis could be tested. Are magnetic interactions the only possible scenario? If so, what sets
the energy scale corresponding to 150 K where the effect turns on. It would also be useful to show
the T-dependent Rxx vs B data for the hybrid device.
7. Measurements of the Hall effect (Rxy) are always tricky because of unavoidable mixing of Rxx contributions into Rxy. The
usual approach is to antisymmetrize the data with respect to the magnetic field direction. The authors need to explain how
they accounted for any possible mixing of Rxx into Rxy. This could play an important role in interpreting signatures
associated with chirality.
8. It would be useful to extract the carrier type and density from the Hall data for some temperatures for the hybrid and control
samples.
9. The authors use Fig. 5 (c) to conclude that hole carriers predominantly contribute to the ordinary Hall effect. However, the
Rxy vs B is non-linear. Have the authors made a two carrier fit to extract information about multiple carrier contributions?
Could they provide estimates of the relevant characteristics (carrier density, mobility)? Given the parallel conduction
channels in this heterostructure, this is of course likely to be difficult to interpret but would be useful to know.
10. The authors refer to a ‘topological Hall effect’ with reference to Fig. 5 (d). However, this is far from clear: what aspects of
this data might lead the authors to claim the presence of a topological Hall effect? The most obvious signature of the
topological Hall effect is an excess Hall voltage above the anomalous and ordinary Hall effects. This has to be carefully
extracted and is not obviously present, even to an experienced eye. To make this attribution requires many more elaborate
tests.
11. The experimental section on the symmetry of Rxy needs to be more clearly written and needs more references. For
example, why are the experimental observations evidence of “chirality”? This is not at all clear. Also, what do the authors
mean by “higher order symmetry” in this context?
